meta.title: Cloud Attack Chain: SSRF to Account Takeover

views.label: Trick the app
views.note: The payload isn't code — it's a URL the vulnerable app fetches on the attacker's behalf.

views.label: Reach the metadata service
views.note: Acting as the attacker's proxy, the app asks the instance metadata service for role credentials.

views.label: Credentials leak back
views.note: The temporary credentials ride the SSRF response all the way back to the attacker.

views.label: Stolen creds hit the cloud API
views.note: If the instance role is over-privileged, those credentials are the whole account.

segments.label: 2. Stolen creds hit the cloud API

messages.label: SSRF: fetch http://169.254.169.254/...
messages.note: the payload is just a URL parameter the app fetches on the attacker's behalf

messages.label: GET .../iam/security-credentials/<role>
messages.note: IMDSv1: no token required to ask

messages.label: SSRF response body leaks the JSON
messages.note: the attacker now holds valid temporary credentials

messages.label: aws s3 ls --profile stolen
messages.note: creds are valid until they expire — often hours

messages.label: 200 OK: full account access
messages.note: an over-privileged instance role = blast radius is the whole account

cards.title: SSRF -> cloud takeover
items: The exploit never touches code — it's one URL the vulnerable app fetches for the attacker
169.254.169.254 is the instance metadata service: no auth, reachable only from inside the box
An over-privileged role turns one SSRF bug into full account access

cards.title: Class check
items: Why doesn't the metadata endpoint need a password?
What single setting (IMDSv2) blocks this exact chain?
Why does the instance role's privilege level decide the blast radius?
